description: I Am The Cavalry talks from BSides Las Vegas 2023.

talks.title: A Hacker’s Guide for Changing The World (and Where do we go from Here?)
talks.teaser: Reflects on a decade of public-interest security advocacy, with practical lessons on policy, influence and scaling impact.
talks.summary:
The closing session of the I Am The Cavalry track at BSides Las Vegas 2023 was a reflective, interactive discussion led by Josh Corman and Beau Woods, marking the group's first decade. They framed the work as a series of experiments in advocacy, covering empathy, storytelling and building common ground with people who hold power. They also described early attempts to reach regulators and Congress that were often dismissed or misunderstood.

The middle of the session moved through practical tools for changing policy. The speakers described the five motivations they see among hackers, the theory of constraints as a way to find the bottleneck that limits progress, and the value of short, memorable frameworks. They walked through how government is structured, including critical infrastructure sectors, sector risk agencies and the difference between voluntary and mandatory security requirements. Their example of a five-point automotive safety framework showed how small, simple ideas can later appear in formal policy documents.

The closing portion turned to what comes next: whether to scale through mentoring, a possible boot camp or an academic body of knowledge, and a focus on rural hospitals and utilities that lack resources. The speakers also raised the risk of volunteer efforts becoming a permanent crutch for problems that need owners. Audience members added ideas, including a suggestion for a textbook-style body of knowledge. The takeaway for practitioners is that lasting change depends on relationships, clear framing and persistence.

talks.title: Public Service Journeys (To and From Hacking Culture)
talks.teaser: Traces how a former Air Force pilot and a policy intern bridged hacker communities and US government work.
talks.summary:
The session is a pair of origin stories from two speakers who reached the hacker community from different directions. One spent 24 years as an Air Force pilot before moving into cybersecurity work at the Pentagon and in the private sector. The other began as a graduate intern and later worked on homeland security programs. Both see their paths as a way of translating between technical researchers and the policy makers who write rules about them.

The middle traces how the Aerospace Village grew out of an aviation cyber initiative. Researchers struggled to get manufacturers to act on flaws, and government had little sense of what the community was doing. A neutral federal party helped run disclosure conversations, and the village became a place where agencies could meet researchers directly. The speakers then describe a COVID-era task force that mapped vaccine supply chains and found overlooked dependencies, such as single-source components and cold storage materials. Smaller organizations were offered free federal scanning services.

The closing advice is practical: build relationships before a crisis, bring diverse voices into policy work because later fixes are slow and costly, expect change to take years, and plan for burnout in long efforts.

talks.title: Introduction to the Track, Reflections on a Decade of IATC
talks.teaser: Looks back at a decade of public-interest security work and its effect on medical device and IoT policy.
talks.summary:
This opening session of the I Am The Cavalry track at BSides Las Vegas marked the group's tenth year. The lead speaker, Jen Ellis, could not attend in person, so her recorded address was played. The presenters framed the session as a retrospective on where the effort began ten years earlier, when concern about connected devices affecting public safety prompted a call for researchers and practitioners to work with regulators and manufacturers.

Much of the talk traced how policy has shifted over that period. Ellis described early pressure on security researchers from legal threats and anti-hacking statutes, and how conversations with lawmakers gradually made the value of research clear. The presenters described a small medical device security meeting held in a hotel room as an early step, which led to work on device guidance, a recall, and eventually the PATCH Act becoming law. They also pointed to an IoT cybersecurity improvement act, a federal task force during the pandemic, and staffers who came through the community and later took roles in Congress and the White House.

The closing portion looked at what remains. The presenters said progress has been uneven, that many connected systems still cannot be patched, and that the effort needs a new phase. They announced a planned gathering to set direction for the next decade and previewed the day's sessions on electrical, food, water and emergency care. The main takeaway is that lasting policy change came from sustained relationships between practitioners and government, and that the work is far from finished.

talks.title: Hungry, Hungry Hackers: A Hacker’s Eye-view of the Food Supply
talks.teaser: Traces how security research into farm equipment changed attitudes toward safety-critical risk in the food supply.
talks.summary:
Casey Ellis presented this session in place of Sick Codes, who could not travel to the event. The talk follows how security research into agricultural equipment shifted how an industry thinks about safety-critical systems. It starts with a flaw in a John Deere customer system that exposed account details to anyone holding a free developer account, and with the vendor's first response, which downplayed the problem.

The middle section covers the follow-on work: a jailbreak of a tractor head unit, a dispute over a private bounty that offered no real disclosure path, and a backdoor found in TCL televisions that later drew attention from federal agencies. The discussion also looks at incidents such as the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack and the JBS breach, and how they pushed critical infrastructure and agricultural connectivity up the agenda. John Deere eventually ran its own challenges and opened a disclosure program.

In the question round, the speaker argues that any organization needs a way to receive outside vulnerability reports, that private-only programs built around NDAs are not true disclosure, and that researchers should start with private outreach while considering how the vendor will react. The takeaway is that research into physical and safety-relevant systems carries real consequences, so it needs a deliberate path to the people who can fix it.

talks.title: Farm to Fork(ed): The Forces Fueling Food Chain Risk
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss how market concentration, weather and cross-sector dependencies make food and agriculture vulnerable to cyber risk.
talks.summary:
The panel, facilitated by Paul F. Roberts, opens by framing agriculture and food as a very large sector that has received little cybersecurity attention. Speakers point to the economic scale of farms, processors and restaurants, and to a growing reliance on connected, remotely managed equipment. Recent ransomware incidents against meat processors, agricultural cooperatives and a produce company are cited as evidence that criminal groups and state actors have turned their attention to the sector.

The middle of the discussion focuses on why the sector is hard to secure. Machinery built for isolated operation now runs on networked software, vendors have commercial reasons to add remote features, and the industry is both widely distributed and concentrated among a few large players. Panelists compare regulation in Europe with emerging proposals in the United States, and they note how food depends on water, power, transport and cold storage. They also describe the thin security capacity of small producers and the shortage of technicians in rural areas. A recurring theme is that availability and recovery timing matter more than confidentiality, since a missed planting or harvest window cannot be recovered later.

The closing exchanges weigh efficiency against resilience. Precision agriculture saves money and time, but panelists argue that fragile designs can be the most profitable, so regulation and secure-by-design requirements may be needed. They also warn that manual fallback skills are fading and that many farmers do not know what data their connected equipment transmits. The main takeaways are the need for sector-specific knowledge of physical processes and baseline security practices that small operators can realistically adopt.

talks.title: Saving Lives in Healthcare
talks.teaser: Explores how security work in healthcare can help protect patients and save lives.

talks.title: Introduction to IATC Day Two
talks.teaser: Previews the second day of the IATC track, covering UK IoT policy, FDA medical device lessons and a hacker guide.
talks.summary:
This short opening segment starts the second day of the IATC track at BSides Las Vegas 2023. Josh Corman, one of the group's founders, frames the day's schedule. He argues that dependence on connected technology is growing faster than the ability to secure it, especially where it touches public safety, human life, the economy and national security.

He outlines three blocks. The first is a session with British colleagues on basic IoT security hygiene and policy they are considering. The second is a retrospective with a US Food and Drug Administration official on a decade of medical device security work, including how regulators approached the community and what they were concerned about. The third is a planned session on distilling the core beliefs and practices behind successful movements into a repeatable guide, possibly a future academy or bootcamp for public-interest security work.

A recorded message from a law professor who has supported the group since its early days is also played. She compares the track's goals to historical cases where public harm led to professional self-regulation, peer review and legal liability in engineering. The takeaway for practitioners is that the track is focused on turning past policy wins into reusable methods, and that the organizers are looking for audience input and volunteers to help shape what comes next.

talks.title: Energy Poverty and Potential Impacts to Other Critical Infrastructures
talks.teaser: Explores how underfunded rural electric co-ops struggle to secure grids amid energy transition, funding gaps and shared responsibility.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speakers' careers in the electric sector and frames the central problem: utilities must become clean, reliable, equitable, resilient and secure at the same time. The United States has roughly 3,000 electric utilities, most of them small, including about 900 rural cooperatives, and some have no one dedicated to security. The history runs from 1930s rural electrification through smart grid spending, the 2013 Metcalf substation attack, the Colonial Pipeline restart, and recent storms and shootings at transformers.

The middle section looks at money and responsibility. Many households struggle to pay their energy bills, and federal clean energy funding is far larger than federal cybersecurity funding. The speakers describe a firmware problem with solar inverters in Hawaii, rooftop devices whose owners are told to firewall them, and a ransomware attack on a 7,000-customer utility handled by a single overloaded employee. They ask who is legally responsible for keeping the lights on when distributed devices belong to others, and they raise concerns about foreign-made inverters with remote radio access.

The closing section offers possible directions. These include defining critical infrastructure by region rather than by utility type, setting a stable and achievable baseline of security goals, and giving small operators decision support instead of more products. Other ideas are cyber-informed engineering, limiting how many devices of one brand connect to a feeder, clearer sensor data standards, and regional support centers that pair students with small utilities. The speakers conclude that solving this will take more than people inside the electric sector.

talks.title: Water, Water Everywhere: The Krakens, Kelpies, and Mermaids in today’s Water Sector
talks.teaser: Walks through the security and operational risks facing water utilities and how failures can ripple into other critical sectors.
talks.summary:
Dean Ford, an automation engineer with decades of control systems work, opens with the basics of water. Only about 2.5 percent of Earth's water is fresh, and less than a third of that is practically reachable. The United States has more than 151,000 public water systems, most of them local and loosely connected, so a failure often becomes a local outage rather than a regional cascade. He then shows who draws on water, with thermoelectric power and irrigation as the largest withdrawals, and hospitals as customers that cannot go without supply even briefly.

The middle of the talk covers threats beyond hacking. He describes scarcity, aging buried pipe, contaminants such as PFAS, sewer overflows, and staff turnover that takes knowledge of valves and procedures out the door with retiring operators. Utilities often cannot raise rates, so they struggle to pay for upgrades. On the cyber side he cites legacy controllers and radios with weak or no authentication, and purchases made without security review. He argues that the 2023 Jackson, Mississippi failure came from underfunding and staffing rather than weather, and that cyber is one risk among many.

For takeaways, he suggests that cyber funding can pay for broader resilience work, that digital twins could preserve operating knowledge and serve as training tools, and that OT, IT and engineering should be managed together with fewer, better-trained staff. He also notes that European NIS2 rules bring water into supply-chain scrutiny, and argues that downstream manufacturers relying on water should help pay for its security. The session closes with audience questions on semiconductor plants' water demand and recovery from attacks on pressure systems.
